editorNote: Atari begins its next life under Jack Tramiel with the old Commodore rivalry no longer confined to the showroom. Around it, video, portable hardware, modems and a swelling IBM-compatible market show how quickly the personal-computer business is widening.
morningLine: Atari and Commodore lawyer up while summer buyers compare games, graphics and machines that travel.

lead.headline: Atari-Commodore Rivalry Turns into a Fight over Trade Secrets
lead.dek: Days after Jack Tramiel takes control of Atari’s consumer operation, his old rivalry with Commodore shifts from price cuts and product launches to engineers, designs and the courts.
body: The struggle for the home-computer market acquired a legal edge this week. On July 14, The New York Times reported a dispute over Commodore trade secrets, arriving only days after Warner Communications transferred Atari’s home-computer and video-game businesses to a company led by former Commodore chief Jack Tramiel.

The sale instantly made Atari and Commodore a rivalry with unusually personal stakes. Tramiel had built Commodore into a mass-market computer power before leaving the company in January; now he was assembling a team to revive Atari’s consumer business and develop a successor to its aging 8-bit machines.

Engineering talent and proprietary designs therefore mattered as much as shelf price. Any movement of former Commodore people into the new Atari could affect how quickly Tramiel’s company produced competitive hardware, while Commodore had every reason to protect work already under way.

The contest unfolded against a harsh financial backdrop. Contemporary UPI reports described Atari’s consumer operation as loss-plagued, and another 300 Sunnyvale employees were dismissed on July 6. The cuts underscored the urgency behind the acquisition: Atari needed fewer costs, fresh products and a credible route back to buyers.

For players and home-computer owners, the courtroom language pointed toward the next hardware race. The familiar Atari and Commodore names would remain on store shelves, but the people, designs and strategies behind them were being rearranged at extraordinary speed.
lead.confidence: Exact-week reporting supported by contemporaneous New York Times and UPI coverage.

stories.headline: BYTE Puts Computers and Video in the Spotlight
body: BYTE’s July issue made “Computers and Video” its central theme, picturing a multichannel workstation and treating moving images as serious personal-computer territory. The $3.50 issue joined video hardware with programming, graphics and communications coverage.

The package catches an important shift: home and small-business machines were no longer discussed only as calculators, word processors or game boxes. Video production and computer-controlled imagery were becoming plausible creative applications, even if the required equipment remained specialized.
For readers following graphics chips, frame grabbers and display standards, BYTE’s feature package offered a map of a field moving toward the desktop.

stories.headline: Sinclair Warns QL Buyers of Delivery Delays
body: Sinclair Research warned that it might struggle to meet the 28-day delivery period printed on QL order forms, according to the July issue of Sinclair User. The company blamed unexpectedly heavy demand.

The delay was especially awkward because the £399 QL was pitched as an ambitious low-cost step beyond 8-bit home machines. Its Motorola 68008 processor, 128 KB of memory and twin Microdrives promised a compact route into more advanced computing.

A bold specification sheet only matters when machines reach customers. Production pressure now threatened the QL’s chance to establish itself against Apple, IBM-compatible and Commodore systems already commanding attention.

stories.headline: PC Magazine Surveys a Fast-Growing IBM Ecosystem
body: The July 10 issue of PC Magazine arrived with another thick snapshot of the IBM PC world. Software, peripherals and compatible systems were multiplying beyond IBM’s own catalog, giving offices more choices and vendors a rapidly expanding audience.

The growth of that ecosystem was becoming the platform’s central advantage. A buyer could increasingly select among competing applications, add-on boards and printers while expecting the PC architecture to remain the common reference point.
For smaller computer makers, the magazine’s advertising and editorial density carried a warning: compatibility was turning into a market of its own, not merely a feature on a specification sheet.
stories.confidence: Exact-date issue reference; broad ecosystem claims are period-contextual.

undergroundDesk.headline: 2600 Reads a Culture of Computer Fear
undergroundDesk.dek: A young hacker and phone-phreak newsletter records the anxiety gathering around anyone with a keyboard and a modem.
body: The July issue of 2600 carried the cover line “Look Out, He’s Got a Computer!” and treated public suspicion of computer users as news within the emerging underground scene.
The item is cultural evidence, not a report of a specific intrusion. Its tone shows how curiosity, technical play and fears about unauthorized access were becoming tangled in the public imagination.
For the growing modem community, the argument was also about identity: whether independent experimenters would be viewed as enthusiasts, nuisances or criminals.
